nameStory: The 'lady's-mantle' name comes from the plant's distinctive leaves, which are shaped like the flowing cloak or mantle that medieval ladies wore. The 'velvet' part refers to the soft, fuzzy hairs covering the leaves and stems that give the plant a plush, velvety texture when you touch it.
description: Velvet Lady's-mantle is a low-growing perennial herb in the rose family, though you'd never guess it's related to roses by looking at it! This European native forms small clumps with distinctive rounded, lobed leaves covered in soft hairs. The plant produces tiny, inconspicuous yellowish-green flowers in loose clusters during summer, but it's really grown for its attractive foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rounded leaves with 7-9 shallow lobes radiating from the center like fingers on a hand, covered in soft hairs that make them feel velvety to touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers without petals, clustered in loose, airy sprays that rise above the foliage on hairy stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mounds or mats, typically 6-12 inches tall and wide, with leaves arising from the base on long stalks

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: All parts of the plant feel distinctly soft and fuzzy due to dense, fine hairs covering leaves and stems

idTips.label: Water Droplets
idTips.description: Morning dew collects beautifully in perfect spherical droplets on the velvety leaf surface, rolling around like mercury

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, found in only a couple of locations as an escape from cultivation. When it does appear, look for it in partially shaded garden borders, rocky slopes, or disturbed areas near old homesites where it may have been planted and persisted.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as fuzzy, folded clusters that gradually unfold into their distinctive lobed shape. The velvety texture is most pronounced on young growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full leaf development and tiny flower clusters appearing on tall, hairy stalks above the foliage mound.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, though some foliage often persists into early winter in protected spots.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, with only the root system surviving underground until spring growth resumes.

funFact: The velvety hairs on Lady's-mantle leaves create a special water-repelling surface that causes morning dew to form perfect, rolling droplets that medieval alchemists believed had magical properties - which is why the scientific name 'Alchemilla' literally means 'little alchemist'!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Garden Lady's-mantle, but Velvet Lady's-mantle is much more hairy and fuzzy to touch, while Garden Lady's-mantle has smoother leaves with just soft hairs along the edges. Remember: velvet = very hairy all over.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, Lady's-mantles look nothing like typical roses - they're more closely related to cinquefoils and strawberries. The tiny flowers lack petals entirely, having only sepals and stamens, which is unusual in this showy family.
compareHints: Velvet Lady's-mantle is distinguished from other Lady's-mantles by its exceptionally hairy, truly velvety texture throughout. Garden Lady's-mantle is larger and less hairy, while the parsley-pierts have much more deeply divided, feathery leaves rather than the broad, rounded lobes of true Lady's-mantles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Garden lady's-mantle is much larger and more robust than its relatives like slender parsley-piert, which has tiny divided leaves and grows as a small annual weed.
Slender parsley-piert differs dramatically from its showy cousin Garden Lady's-mantle, which has large, soft leaves and grows over a foot tall.
Thin-stem Lady's-mantle is distinguished from Garden Lady's-mantle by its much more delicate build and notably slender stems.
